Virtuous Woman
VUR-choo-us WOOM-an
noun phrase (Proverbs 31)
From the Latin virtus (strength, worth), rendering the Hebrew 'eshet chayil, “a woman of strength, worth, or valour”; the closing portrait of Proverbs.

📖 Biblical Definition

The virtuous woman is the crowning portrait of the book of Proverbs, the acrostic poem of chapter thirty-one that sets forth the godly wife and mother as a woman of strength and worth whose price is far above rubies. The Hebrew 'eshet chayil describes not a passive ornament but a woman of valour: she works willingly with her hands, riseth while it is yet night to give meat to her household, considereth a field and buyeth it, planteth a vineyard, stretcheth out her hand to the poor and needy, maketh fine linen and selleth it, openeth her mouth with wisdom, and in her tongue is the law of kindness. The heart of her husband doth safely trust in her; her children arise up and call her blessed; her husband praiseth her in the gates. The poem refuses the world's twin lies about womanhood—that worth lies in favour and beauty, which are deceitful and vain, and that the home is a small and slighted sphere. Her industry, enterprise, and strength are poured out within and from the household she governs, and the secret of all of it is named in the final verse: a woman that feareth the LORD, she shall be praised. The dictionary holds this chapter as the biblical standard of femininity over against both the older sentimentality that made the wife a frail decoration and the newer ideology that despises the home; she is strong, capable, and praised, and she is so as a wife and mother who fears God in the complementary order of creation.

📜 Webster 1828 Definition

The Hebrew 'eshet chayil, the “woman of valour” of Proverbs 31, whose strength, industry, and wisdom are poured out in the fear of the LORD; the biblical standard of godly womanhood.

expand to see more

VIRTUOUS WOMAN, noun phrase. [Hebrew 'eshet chayil, a woman of strength or worth.] The godly wife and mother portrayed in Proverbs 31.

Her price is far above rubies; the heart of her husband safely trusteth in her.

She works willingly with her hands, governs her household, deals in field and merchandise, and stretches out her hand to the poor.

She openeth her mouth with wisdom, and the law of kindness is in her tongue.

Favour is deceitful and beauty vain, but a woman that feareth the LORD shall be praised.

📖 Key Scripture

Pr 31:10 — "Who can find a virtuous woman? for her price is far above rubies."

Pr 31:11 — "The heart of her husband doth safely trust in her, so that he shall have no need of spoil."

Pr 31:30 — "Favour is deceitful, and beauty is vain: but a woman that feareth the LORD, she shall be praised."

Ru 3:11 — "And now, my daughter, fear not; I will do to thee all that thou requirest: for all the city of my people doth know that thou art a virtuous woman."

⚠️ Modern Corruption

The portrait is corrupted both by an older sentimentality that made the wife a frail ornament and by a newer ideology that despises the home and recasts her industry as proof against the complementary order.

expand to see more

Modern egalitarian readings seize on the virtuous woman's commerce and enterprise to argue that Proverbs 31 overturns the complementary order of Scripture, as though her field-buying and merchandising proved the home an unworthy sphere. The dictionary names this as a corruption of the passage. The woman of valour is praised precisely as a wife whose husband's heart trusts in her and as a mother whose children call her blessed; her strength is poured out within and from a household she governs under her husband's headship. Her capability is no argument against the created order but the flowering of a woman who fears the LORD inside it.

The opposite corruption is the older sentimentality that made the godly wife a frail and idle decoration, valued for favour and beauty—the very things the poem calls deceitful and vain. Scripture's woman is strong, industrious, wise, and generous, rising before dawn and opening her mouth with wisdom. The dictionary recovers the whole portrait: neither a feminist proof-text nor a Victorian ornament, but a woman of valour whose worth is her fear of God and whose sphere is the household and all that flows from it.

🔗 Greek & Hebrew Roots

From the Hebrew 'eshet chayil, a woman of chayil (strength, force, worth, valour), the same word used of mighty men of war; the Latin virtus behind “virtuous” carries the same note of strength.

expand to see more

'Ishshah, Hebrew, woman or wife, the subject of the acrostic poem.

Chayil, Hebrew, strength, force, worth, ability—used elsewhere of armies and valiant men.

Virtus, Latin, strength and worth, the root of the English “virtuous,” which once meant powerful, not merely well-behaved.

The acrostic form (each verse beginning with a successive Hebrew letter) frames her praise as an ordered whole.

The same word chayil is spoken over Ruth (Ruth 3:11), binding the Moabitess to the ideal of Proverbs 31.

Usage

"He preached Proverbs 31 to honour the labouring mothers of the congregation as women of valour, not idle ornaments."

"She taught her daughters that favour and beauty fade, but the fear of the LORD makes a woman praised."

"The elder rebuked the notion that the home is a small sphere, pointing to all the virtuous woman governs from it."
